data.title: Classified NSA network is still down, leaving some staff working from home
data.description: An internal classified computer network used by the National Security Agency remained down on Thursday, resulting in some employees being ordered to work from home for a third day in a row, according to two people with knowledge of the matter. The network first went down on Tuesday due to a technical problem that occurred when maintenance on the network was underway. Both sources told NBC News the issue has created an inconvenience, but it has not affected the NSA’s work collecting electronic intelligence around the world and overseeing cyber security. There is no sign that the outage was caused by a cyber attack, the sources said. Even though the NSA’s network issue came amid an unusual series of mass outages that have wreaked havoc on air travel, banks and emails over the past few days, U.S. officials have said say there is no indication that the technical problems were caused by a coordinated cyberattack. Non-essential staff at the NSA are being told to check in with their supervisors and find out if they need to come into the agency’s headquarters at Fort Meade, Maryland. Otherwise, they are advised to work from home, according to a telephone information line for the workforce and the two sources familiar with the matter. While the NSA does not release the precise number of agency employees, former officials have said the agency employs tens of thousands of people. In 2024, a Maryland state government document put the number of NSA employees at 39,000. The agency has since made some workforce reductions as part of broader cutbacks across the federal government. The outage also affected a work site in Georgia that handles the NSA’s electronic intelligence work in the Middle East, the sources said. In a statement Tuesday, the NSA acknowledged experiencing a “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance.” “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues,” the statement reads. “NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.” The NSA, which oversees the nation’s vast electronic surveillance efforts, is considered one of the world’s most sophisticated cyber security and electronic spy agencies. With powerful eavesdropping and code-breaking tools as well as a well-educated workforce, the NSA prides itself as a center of digital expertise. While it is not uncommon for government networks to suffer from brief disruptions or outages, such a high-profile technical problem threatens to tarnish that reputation the agency has built, according to former officials and experts.

data.title: Trump touts ‘unbelievable’ summit with Putin and Xi, though peace deals remain elusive
data.description: SHENZHEN, China — Back home, President Donald Trump faces low approval ratings and a resurgent Democratic opposition, but for a couple of satisfying days abroad, he got the respect he relishes. When Trump arrived in China on Wednesday, the country’s leader, Xi Jinping, broke precedent and came out to the tarmac to greet him. And before Trump boarded Air Force One to return home, he strode along a red carpet as a military regiment stood at attention. “Everything was unbelievable ... they treated me as well as the person could be treated,” Trump said in a phone interview with NBC News as he flew home. Coming off the Democrats’ sweeping victory in the midterm elections on Nov. 3, the White House felt compelled to post an image alerting Americans that Trump is “still your president.” Trump’s Chinese hosts needed no such reminders. They arranged a memorable bit of stagecraft on Thursday, placing Trump, Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin at an oversized, bagel-shaped table, leaving an impression that the leaders of the world’s nuclear and economic powers were deciding humanity’s future. If there was one image to counteract the notion that Trump is a lame duck whose power is seeping away as Democrats regain control of Congress, that might have been it. Elevating Putin as he wages a grinding war with Ukraine is a gamble for Trump. Much of the international community made Putin a pariah following his annexation of Crimea in 2014 and full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Blowback has been coming Trump’s way, after he agreed to trilateral and bilateral meetings with Russia’s leader and worked the Ukraine conflict into those conversations. Previewing the meetings ahead of the visit, a U.S. official had said the war wouldn’t be raised. In the interview with NBC, Trump said that the summit was, “on a scale of zero to 10 … a 12. It was a great summit and very important. Fantastic relationships built and you know the meetings were good, but the final two and the final three were just amazing, amazing meetings.” Though the leaders discussed the Iran war — “they’d like it to end ... and they’re letting Iran know that” — the meeting “was primarily on Ukraine, obviously,” Trump said. Whether the sit-downs will culminate in a peace deal is far from clear. Two of Trump’s special envoys, his son-in-law Jared Kushner and longtime friend Steve Witkoff, were heading to Berlin on Thursday for meetings with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in hopes of a breakthrough. Since taking office, Trump has tried without success to end a Russia-Ukraine conflict that he once promised to settle on his first day. In doing so, he has made no secret of his affection for Putin, raising questions about whether he is a fair broker. The two men met separately in Shenzhen before the trilateral meeting with Xi, with Trump calling Putin a “friend.” That triggered a blunt response — in the U.S. and overseas. “I think Putin’s a thug. I think he’s killing babies and people in Ukraine,” Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said Thursday. “I think it’s despicable what he’s done.” Ukraine’s top diplomat in the U.S., Denys Sienik, told NBC News in an interview: “I cannot speak for the president of the United States of America, but as a Ukrainian, Putin is not a friend. Putin is a war criminal.” “Russia attacks Ukraine every single day,” added Sienik, the chargé d’affaires at the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington. “When this meeting with President Trump happened in China, Russia attacked Ukrainian cities including the capital of Ukraine.” The embassy sent NBC News a photo that, it said, showed a Russian drone being shot down over the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Kyiv on Thursday. The mere act of meeting Putin face to face raises Putin’s stature, signaling to world leaders that the Russian leader should no longer be an outcast. That’s a gift from Trump that Putin hasn’t earned, some foreign policy experts said. “Russia wants to be elevated to the big-boys table and send a message to Ukraine that decisions are being made over Ukraine’s head,” Jake Sullivan, who was White House national security adviser under President Joe Biden, told NBC News. That won’t happen, Trump pledged. Zelenskyy told NBC News this week that any deal that Xi, Trump and Putin negotiate won’t succeed unless Ukraine signs on. Trump has quarreled with Zelenskyy in the past, but on that point, he said they’re aligned. “I agree with him,” Trump said in the phone interview. “I wouldn’t do anything without — he’s the head of that country, so I wouldn’t be doing that.” Putin sounded in no mood for peace at a press conference following his meetings with Trump and Xi. This week, Ukraine repeatedly attacked a bridge that links Crimea and Russia. The bridge is a point of pride for Putin, who sees it as a symbol of Russia’s control of Crimea. Putin said that because of the attacks, Russia would not negotiate and that reprisals would be “painful.” Trump said in the phone interview that the bridge attack came up in his meetings and that Putin was upset over it. But Trump added, “That’s the sad part of war.” “You end up ultimately negotiating,” he said. “I think he [Putin] would like to see it ended.” For Putin to relent, he must face more pressure from abroad, Ukrainian leaders argue. That doesn’t appear to be Trump’s calculation. Last month, he lifted U.S. sanctions aimed at drying up sources of Russia’s outside revenue. As for meeting with Xi, Trump said the two discussed artificial intelligence and American agricultural exports. Hard-and-fast deals, though, seem a ways off. “We spoke about SI [Super Intelligence], and we both agreed that we want— we’re, you know, very much into SI, but we do think that having guardrails, you know, at least on a minimal basis is a positive thing,” Trump said, using his favorite term for artificial intelligence. Asked what he meant by a “minimal basis,” Trump said, “Well, we didn’t get into definitions.” Farmers may see a windfall as a result of the meetings, Trump said. “Because of the relationship, they’re buying a lot of the soybeans and corn and stuff, the agricultural products. I think we’re going to have a great, a very substantial increase in that for the farmers,” he said. Does that mean China committed to buying more agricultural products? “I don’t want to say the word ‘commit,’ but yes, I would, I would say ‘commit.’ … I would view it as something that will move very quickly, and we’ll probably get it done. Let me put it that way,” he said. For Trump, the deference shown to him here and in Manila this week seemed a high point of the trip. In a live interview with Fox News that aired Wednesday evening in the U.S., he was asked what “headline” might come out of his meetings with Xi and Putin. “You saw the greeting yesterday, which in the history of China has never happened,” Trump said of Xi meeting him at the airport, a gesture Trump had extended to Xi in Washington earlier this year. “No president has ever — and this is a highly respected, this is a great president, one of the great presidents of China — and he has never gone to the airport to meet somebody.”

data.title: Tech outages have fueled a blackout panic — and a prepping boom
data.description: The end of the world, apparently, comes with a shopping list. On TikTok and Instagram, people are packing emergency bug-out bags, stockpiling canned goods and showing off big-box store hauls as rumors of an impending nationwide blackout spread online.

data.title: Anthropic is about to be worth more than $1 trillion. What that means for the rest of us
data.description: Leading AI lab Anthropic is expected to make the largest-ever public market debut when it starts trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange Thursday. Founded in 2021 by brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei, both former employees of rival OpenAI, Anthropic and its main product, Claude, are seen as the gold standard of AI models, despite lacking the household-name cache of ChatGPT. With a target market value of $1.5 trillion — larger than SpaceX’s record setting IPO just a few months ago — Anthropic’s public arrival will serve as more than just a measure of what Wall Street thinks the company is worth. It will be a test of current sentiment around AI itself at a pivotal moment for the industry. For much of the past year, the AI investment wave has powered the stock market to new heights and sustained U.S. economic growth. But there are signs the wave may be starting to break. “Investors have over recent weeks become increasingly concerned around the sustainability of the investment boom,” James McCann, senior economist for investment strategy at Edward Jones, said in a client note Wednesday ahead of Anthropic’s debut. The market gains notched this spring and summer thanks to the AI boom have now largely been wiped out. Fears of over-spending on infrastructure, rising debt loads, ballooning costs and uncertain demand have grown. At the same time, public opinion has turned against data centers and AI-skeptical Democrats won control of Congress earlier this month. Then, the Jensen Huang scandal broke, creating a cloud of uncertainty over Nvidia, a company at the heart of the AI economy. The tech heavy Nasdaq was up 19% for the year recently. As of Wednesday, it’s higher by less than 5%. “The leadership change at Nvidia meanwhile adds to short-term uncertainty around the sector, particularly given the important role this giant company has played in financially supporting a range of smaller technology firms in recent years,” said McCann. “With the selloff in technology stocks continuing this week investors will be watching to see how well the Anthropic IPO is received.” There is little debate over how uniquely successful Anthropic has been. The latest edition of Claude, dubbed Fable, ranks No. 1 on Artificial Analysis’ leaderboard of top-performing large language models as it is able to handle complex computer engineering tasks. And its Claude Code application is now used throughout the tech industry and by some accounts became the fastest-growing product in enterprise software history when it was released in Feb. 2025, hitting $1 billion in revenues within six months of launching. Thursday’s IPO is also expected to mint a new crop of billionaires and multi-millionaires as Anthropic’s co-founders and early employees see their interest in the company turned into shares with a defined cash value. Part of that will be fueled by a massive appetite for investing in the shares among mom-and-pop investors. According to Vanda Research, a markets consultancy, Anthropic could see approximately $250 million worth of buying among non-institutional or “retail” investors when it starts trading Thursday. That would be double the magnitude of interest following SpaceX’s IPO. Other major winners will include Amazon, Google-parent Alphabet, Microsoft, and Nvidia, which will each own billions-worth of Anthropic shares. Some observers see Anthropic’s debut as more of a major milestone than a make-or-break moment. In their view, there are plenty of other investments backstopping the AI boom. “A strong IPO would help resurrect the AI trade, but it does not mean a weaker-than-expected IPO would bury that trade,” said Renée Friedman, global head of research at EXANTE, a Europe-based finance and technology group. “There are significant commitments into the AI cycle by some of the world’s largest companies over a multi-year period. These are not going to just disappear,” he said. In the first half of 2026, Anthropic saw total revenues of more than $16 billion. That compares with $41 million over the same period just three years ago. While Anthropic was technically operating at a loss to start the year, investors expect it to be profitable soon. Those heady figures capture a tension at the heart of Anthropic’s IPO. In addition to being the leading AI lab, current and former Anthropic employees have also been some of the most vocal proponents of AI safety, giving voice to fears that, should the technology become too advanced, it could start to run amok. “I think that without international coordination we will incur a risk of causing human extinction,” former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon wrote of his concerns about AI shortly before resigning. Yet some critics have said those concerns have proven no match for the seemingly unstoppable momentum of creating a company publicly valued at more than $1 trillion. Dario Amodei has responded, arguing building safe AI and creating the world’s most advanced — and valuable — AI models are not necessarily mutually exclusive. When a user criticized Anthropic for seeming to plunge ahead with its attempt to create “superhuman” AI despite the risks to humanity doing so, Amodei replied in an X post that “a list of things that Anthropic did in the past year that were pro-safety and commercially costly to us” would be much longer than a list of risks it posed to mankind.

data.title: Google faces a reckoning after pushing its AI tools into classrooms
data.description: Over the past two decades, Google has become entwined with almost every aspect of America’s public schools. Millions of students take tests on Chromebooks and use Google’s apps to complete assignments. Teachers turn to the tech giant for free training and conference sponsorships. Now, though, a backlash is brewing.

data.title: National security and AI figures urge DOJ to probe what Nvidia knew about chip smuggling
data.description: A group of 15 national security experts and AI policy leaders is urging the Justice Department to investigate what Nvidia knew about the alleged smuggling of its advanced AI chips to China, and whether the company continued doing business with customers after evidence emerged that they were illegally diverting the technology. The letter, sent Tuesday and addressed to Attorney General Todd Blanche, asks the department to examine whether Nvidia kept selling chips to customers or middlemen after receiving evidence that they were illegally routing them to China, or whether the company “deliberately blinded itself to export control violations.” “The United States has the world’s most advanced SI chip technology, much of it built by Nvidia,” the letter states, using the Trump administration’s “super intelligence” label for AI. “Smuggling operations threaten to undermine that lead, giving China access to hardware necessary for developing advanced SI and deploying it to boost its military capabilities and international influence.” The 15 signatories include a range of national security experts and AI policy specialists, such as David Buckley, the Central Intelligence Agency’s former inspector general; Randy Manner, a retired Army general; Chris McGuire, a former Biden official who specialized in chips; and Brad Carson, the president of Americans for Responsible Innovation, the AI advocacy group that organized the letter. “China and our competitors around the world have their sights set on our advanced AI chips so they can build up their AI capabilities,” Carson told NBC News. “Nvidia’s advanced AI chips are at the top of their wish lists.” Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment. On Tuesday, the company’s board of directors announced that it would establish a committee dedicated to investigating national security and export control compliance. The letter comes amid growing scrutiny of the American chipmaker and calls from Congress to investigate the extent of Nvidia’s awareness of the chips’ destination and whether the company did anything about potential smuggling. On Tuesday, the Justice and Commerce departments shared details about their investigation of Megaspeed, the Singaporean company tied to suspected Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang. Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang is alleged to have had an affair with Megaspeed’s Huang. Megaspeed reportedly acquired billions of dollars’ worth of Nvidia chips and is also being investigated over concerns that it — and its subsidiaries — smuggled chips to China. In a joint statement Tuesday, the agencies said Commerce opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024, requested sales records from Nvidia in May 2025 and that Nvidia placed the company on its no-sell list the following month. Commerce investigators also conducted an in-person inspection of Megaspeed’s facilities with Singaporean law enforcement in June 2025. The Justice Department said it took the lead in the criminal investigation after that enforcement action. The agencies said they would continue working together to pursue any criminal conduct that may have occurred. Huang has agreed to sit for an interview with several national security-focused House committees on Dec. 1, according to House Republicans. The appearance will focus on the former CEO’s role in “a potential breach of our national security,” according to the lawmakers. Tuesday’s letter to Blanche points to several smuggling cases the Justice Department has brought in the past year involving Nvidia. In March 2026, prosecutors charged three people in an alleged scheme in which a Southeast Asian intermediary bought roughly $2.5 billion worth of servers containing advanced AI chips. Prosecutors allege at least $510 million worth were illegally sent to China. “Repeated attempts to route Nvidia chips to China point to a pattern that warrants a closer examination of company practices and how Nvidia responded to repeated alarming discoveries over the past several years regarding the scale of smuggling operations,” the letter states. Smuggled chips are estimated to equal at least 25% of the chips Chinese AI companies obtained through legal routes — though the actual figure may be far larger. Many Chinese companies, including tech titans Alibaba and Tencent, have reportedly also leased chips from data centers based in Singapore, Malaysia and other southeast Asian countries. This week, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and the department’s Bureau of Industry and Security announced that it would close that loophole. The department said it would enact a new set of regulations limiting foreign data centers’ ability to rent their chips to Chinese companies and enacting new requirements for chip customers in five southeast Asian countries — including Singapore and Malaysia — in order to receive chips from American companies like Nvidia or AMD. China criticized the rule. “Such actions run counter to the consensus reached between the two sides, infringe upon the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises, and disrupt the stability of global industrial and supply chains,” foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a regular briefing in Beijing. Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips are widely considered the most powerful available. Under current export rules, Nvidia cannot sell its top-tier chips to China, though it can sell older generation chips, from the H200 family, to China with a 25% fee taken by the White House. The Justice Department established a new body dedicated to cracking down on AI-related crime in early November. This force, called the Super Intelligence Task Force, aims to “ensure that America’s leadership in SI is not compromised by the misuse of SI by foreign state and state-sponsored actors, transnational criminal organizations, and individual or corporate actors engaged in fraud or other unlawful conduct,” according to the Department. Some lawmakers have clamored for stricter rules on advanced AI chip exports to China. Members of the House’s Select Committee on China have sought to restrict China’s ability to purchase chipmaking equipment and to implement stronger chip-tracking technology — to ensure that chips sent to data centers outside mainland China remain outside of the country. Tuesday’s letter closes by urging the department “to follow the evidence wherever it leads and pursue appropriate enforcement action where violations are established.”

data.title: Jeff Bezos says he was ‘heavily involved’ in picking the new James Bond
data.description: Tech billionaire and Amazon founder Jeff Bezos has said that he was “heavily involved” with casting the new James Bond, telling an audience on Tuesday night that actor Robert Pattinson had displayed “something special.” Amazon MGM Studios assumed creative control of the blockbuster franchise last year, tapping Denis Villeneuve to direct its first instalment. In a rare peek into the casting of the iconic British spy, Bezos pulled back the curtain on the selection process that ultimately saw Pattinson announced as 007 to much global fanfare on Monday. “We ran a really tight process and we made the final decision on Friday,” Bezos told Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event in California. A “big group” of contenders were whittled down to five finalists who went through “real, old-fashioned screen tests” Bezos said. He added that the contenders each acted out three different scenes with “full costume, real sets, other actors with them,” to help with the casting process. Bezos did not name the finalists, but actors who reportedly tested for the role included Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor, Jack Lowden and Nicholas Hoult. Bezos said that he and a team, including the movie’s director Villeneuve, spent hours reviewing the finalists on Friday, noting that they were all “extraordinarily talented.” But he said “there was something special about Rob and his performances ... It was immediately un-debated,” he added. “We all gravitated toward Rob.” Pattinson said playing the suave British spy was “the honour of a lifetime.” In a statement on Monday, he added, “to say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.” With a career spanning more than two decades, Pattinson took to the screen as a teenager playing vampire Edward Cullen in the “Twilight” movies and Cedric Diggory in the “Harry Potter” franchise. A distinctive and versatile actor, he went on to pivot between smaller independent films and mega-studio productions including “The Batman.” Pattinson also recently enjoyed a viral turn as villainous Antinous in Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster “The Odyssey,” and played a shapeshifting assassin in “Dune: Part Three,” which saw him work with director Villeneuve. The script for the new Bond film is being written by Steven Knight, who created the British television series “Peaky Blinders.” No release date has yet been given for the new movie. Bond has evolved into one of the most coveted and discussed roles in film, with the book-to-screen character written by Ian Fleming displaying rare staying power across generations. “I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey ... but there can only be one 007,” director Villeneuve said in a statement this week. “I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new.” Bezos said initially the casting team had been “slightly biased” against Pattinson because he is “already so famous” and said they had been seeking “somebody a little more unknown.” Ultimately, he added, “in the screening tests, it was so obvious, he is James Bond.”

data.title: Amid string of outages, bipartisan letter urges strategy to combat AI-assisted cyber threats
data.description: In the midst of a series of recent cyber outages, there is growing concern by members of Congress that the Trump administration needs to do more to protect infrastructure from cyberattacks that are aided by AI, according to a new bipartisan letter sent by two senators to the White House’s AI czar. The letter from U.S. Sens. Maria Cantwell from Washington state, the top Democrat on the Senate Commerce Committee, and Mike Rounds, the Republican from South Dakota who chairs the Senate Armed Services Committee Subcommittee on Cybersecurity, urges AI czar Jay Clayton to develop a new national strategy that addresses AI-assisted cyber threats. “AI is rapidly increasing the ability to discover and exploit weaknesses in software, and our defenses are not keeping pace,” the senators wrote. They noted that AI can quickly find vulnerabilities in software and get around regular cyber defenses. Repair patches that are supposed to protect infrastructure can take weeks or months to test and install. And they wrote that autonomous AI agents can introduce new security risks. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday. It’s not clear what kind of role, if any, AI has played in the ongoing outages impacting U.S. consumers and travelers, but questions are expected to come up when Clayton testifies before the House Committee on Homeland Security on Wednesday morning. Clayton who also serves as the Director of National Intelligence was named to the AI role in early October is leading a task force of government officials to produce an AI policy by the end of January. In their letter to Clayton, the senators cited an ongoing wave of cyberattacks in Japan that have impacted financial institutions and companies, leading “to large-scale data breaches and leaks, which the Japanese government is now seeking to contain.” The string of attacks are believed to be boosted by AI. They also pointed to incidents where rogue artificial intelligence agents have accessed customers’ bank accounts, leaving banks worried that AI could initiate transactions on its own. The senators are asking for Clayton’s task force to bring together AI companies and federal agencies to secure digital infrastructure and develop security standards for autonomous AI agents. Speaking to reporters in the Philippines overnight, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sought to reassure Americans, saying that recent outages such as those that impacted Microsoft Outlook, United Airlines and the Federal Aviation Administration are not connected to one another. “We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind,” he said.
